# List of ports in Ireland

Ara Eve Leo Sal

 1x 

The list of ports in Ireland encompasses the seaports and harbours along the roughly 7,500-kilometre coastline of the island, which includes the [Republic of Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Republic_of_Ireland) and [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), serving as vital infrastructure for [international trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/International_trade), [passenger](https://grokipedia.com/page/Passenger) ferries, bulk cargo handling, and regional connectivity.[[[1]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-1)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-1)In the [Republic of Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Republic_of_Ireland), maritime activities are coordinated through approximately 25 ports and harbour authorities, including state companies (about 7), local authority ports, and other harbours, with major facilities like [Dublin Port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin_Port) and Port of Cork dominating freight throughput.[[[2]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2) These ports handled a total of 47.8 million tonnes of goods in 2023 (revised to 47.6 million tonnes), a 10% decrease from 2022, primarily comprising liquid bulk (such as [petroleum](https://grokipedia.com/page/Petroleum) products), dry bulk (agricultural goods and ores), containerized [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), and roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) traffic, while also accommodating over 2 million [passenger](https://grokipedia.com/page/Passenger)s annually via ferries and cruises.[[[2]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)[[[3]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-3)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-3)[[[4]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-4)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-4) In 2024, throughput increased to 51 million tonnes, a 7% rise, driven by growth in dry bulk and Ro-Ro sectors amid expanding roles in offshore renewables.[[[5]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-5)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-5) Key [Republic](https://grokipedia.com/page/Republic) ports include **[Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin)** (the busiest, managing about 74% of national merchandise trade by volume in 2023), **Cork**, **Shannon Foynes**, **Waterford**, **[Rosslare Europort](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rosslare_Europort)**, and **[Drogheda](https://grokipedia.com/page/Drogheda)**, alongside customs-appointed facilities such as Galway, Limerick, and Sligo for regional and specialized operations.[[[6]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-6)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-6)[[[7]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-7)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-7)[[[8]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)Northern Ireland's port sector, overseen by the Department for Infrastructure, features three principal ports—**[Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast)**, **[Larne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Larne)**, and **[Warrenpoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Warrenpoint)**—which collectively processed 27.8 million tonnes of freight in 2023, accounting for 91.5% of regional traffic and emphasizing Ro-Ro and bulk commodities like aggregates and animal feed.[[[9]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)[Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) Port alone handled 66.3% of Northern Ireland's total tonnage, underscoring its role as a transatlantic gateway, while [Larne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Larne) supports extensive [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) links to [Scotland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scotland) and [England](https://grokipedia.com/page/England), handling the majority of the approximately 570,000 non-freight vehicles passing through Northern Ireland ports in 2023.[[[9]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9) Together, these ports across the island facilitated over 75 million tonnes of annual cargo in 2023, bolstering sectors like manufacturing, agriculture, and energy, while adhering to [EU](https://grokipedia.com/page/.eu) and [UK](https://grokipedia.com/page/United_Kingdom) customs protocols post-Brexit.[[[2]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)[[[9]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9) Smaller harbours and marinas, such as those in Wexford, [Tralee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tralee), and Foyle Port, complement the network by supporting fisheries, leisure boating, and local supply chains.[[[6]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-6)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-6)[[[10]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-10)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-10)
## Background

### Port Classification

A port in Ireland is defined as a maritime facility equipped to handle [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), passengers, [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) vessels, or recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) activities, serving as a critical interface between sea and land transport networks.Under Ireland's National Ports Policy, established in 2013 and subject to an ongoing review process initiated in 2023, with the final revised policy anticipated in the first half of [2026](https://grokipedia.com/page/2026), commercial ports are classified into tiers based on their scale, trade volume, and national importance. Tier 1 ports, designated for national and international significance, include Dublin Port Company, Port of Cork Company, and Shannon Foynes Port Company; these facilities collectively handle the majority of the country's freight and passenger traffic. Tier 2 ports, focused on regional significance and supporting competitive markets in specific sectors, comprise Port of Waterford Company and [Rosslare Europort](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rosslare_Europort). Additional commercial ports of regional importance, such as [Drogheda](https://grokipedia.com/page/Drogheda) Port Company and Galway Harbour Company, fall outside the Tier 1 and Tier 2 categories but contribute to localized trade and logistics.[[[11]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)[[[12]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-12)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-12)[[[13]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-13)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-13)Beyond the tiered commercial ports, Ireland recognizes specialized classifications for other maritime facilities. Fishing harbors, known as Fishery Harbour Centres, are designated and managed by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine to support sea fishing, fish processing, and related activities; examples include Killybegs and Castletownbere, which are maintained as multi-purpose assets for the fishing industry. Yacht marinas and recreational harbors cater primarily to leisure boating and are often operated by local authorities or private entities, emphasizing berthing and support services rather than commercial cargo. Cruise terminals, integrated within larger commercial ports, are equipped for passenger vessels and tourism, with facilities designed for efficient embarkation and shore excursions.[[[14]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)[[[15]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-15)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-15)In [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), ports are overseen by the Department for Infrastructure without a formal tier system akin to the Republic's policy, instead categorized broadly as commercial or local harbors to facilitate [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) and regional connectivity. Major commercial ports, such as [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) Harbour and [Larne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Larne) Harbour, function as key [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) gateways handling significant cargo and passenger volumes, while smaller local harbors support fishing and community needs; trust ports like [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) and [Warrenpoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Warrenpoint) operate under statutory oversight to ensure public benefit.[[[16]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-16)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-16)[[[17]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-17)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-17)The classification criteria for Irish ports emphasize quantitative and qualitative factors, including annual [tonnage](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tonnage) handled—typically with Tier 1 ports exceeding several million tonnes—to gauge economic impact, alongside [infrastructure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infrastructure) attributes like [water](https://grokipedia.com/page/Water) depth for vessel access (often 10-15 meters or more for larger ports) and strategic positioning within [EU](https://grokipedia.com/page/.eu) trade corridors. These elements ensure ports align with national objectives for efficient [maritime transport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Maritime_transport) and resilience in global supply chains.[[[11]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)[[[18]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-18)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-18)
### Economic and Strategic Importance

Irish ports serve as the primary conduits for the country's external trade, handling over 95% of merchandise by volume as an island nation reliant on maritime logistics. In 2024, total [goods](https://grokipedia.com/page/Goods) throughput across major ports reached 51 million tonnes, reflecting a 7% increase from the previous year and underscoring the sector's resilience amid global [supply chain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Supply_chain) pressures.[[[19]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-19)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-19) This volume includes a mix of bulk commodities, containerized [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), and roll-on/roll-off traffic essential for Ireland's export-driven economy.The maritime sector, which includes port operations, shipping, and ancillary services, makes a substantial contribution to [Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ireland)'s GDP. Valued at €2.7 billion in [gross value added](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gross_value_added) in 2023 (up from €1.6 billion in 2021), it supports approximately 20,000 direct jobs and underpins annual trade flows exceeding €100 billion, primarily through imports of raw materials and exports of high-value goods like pharmaceuticals and agri-products. These activities not only drive [regional development](https://grokipedia.com/page/Regional_development) but also enhance national competitiveness by connecting [Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ireland) to global markets.[[[20]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-20)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-20)Strategically, Irish ports have evolved as critical gateways for EU-UK trade following [Brexit](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brexit), managing rerouted flows and maintaining seamless supply chains under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. They also facilitate vital ferry links to Britain and continental Europe, carrying around 4 million passengers annually and supporting tourism and short-sea shipping. Emerging as hubs for offshore wind energy, ports are positioning to support Ireland's target of 5 GW installed capacity by 2030, with infrastructure upgrades enabling assembly, maintenance, and deployment of renewable projects.[[[21]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-21)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-21)[[[22]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-22)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-22)In [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), ports handle approximately 95% of the region's external trade, with [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) Harbour alone processing 24.1 million tonnes in 2024, a slight rise from the prior year and vital for cross-border and international commerce. This throughput bolsters local industries and mitigates economic isolation post-Brexit.[[[9]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)[[[23]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-23)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-23)Looking ahead, Irish ports face challenges like decarbonization, with initiatives such as [shore power](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shore_power) adoption at facilities like [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) and Rosslare aimed at reducing emissions from idling vessels through EU-funded projects. Efforts to mitigate port congestion include capacity expansions and digitalization, while alignment with the EU's [Trans-European Transport Network](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trans-European_Transport_Network) (TEN-T) grants core and comprehensive status to key ports, unlocking funding for sustainable upgrades.[[[24]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-24)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-24)[[[25]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-25)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-25)
## Ports by Coastal Region

### East Coast Ports

The east coast ports of Ireland, bordering the [Irish Sea](https://grokipedia.com/page/Irish_Sea), serve as vital gateways for passenger ferries linking the island to Britain and for industrial cargo transport, including bulk commodities, containers, and roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) freight essential to EU-UK [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) routes. These facilities, ranging from major commercial hubs to specialized [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure) harbors, handle a significant portion of Ireland's maritime activity, with emphasis on efficient cross-sea connectivity and support for sectors like [construction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Construction), [agriculture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Agriculture), and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism). Ports in this region benefit from proximity to Dublin's [economic corridor](https://grokipedia.com/page/Economic_corridor), facilitating just-in-time [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics) while facing challenges from tidal constraints and urban development pressures.**Arklow Port**, situated in [County Wicklow](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Wicklow) midway between [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) and Rosslare, functions as a commercial harbor primarily serving the maritime industry with dry bulk trade, including timber and aggregates for [construction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Construction). It supports local shipping operations and offshore activities, such as servicing the nearby Arklow Bank windfarm, though its depth limitations restrict larger vessels. The port is managed by Wicklow [County Council](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_council) and remains a key asset for regional export-import flows.[[[26]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-26)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-26)**Belfast Port** in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland) stands as one of the region's premier commercial facilities, specializing in Ro-Ro freight to Britain, containers, and [bulk cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bulk_cargo) like [coal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Coal) and [grain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Grain), with an annual throughput of 24.1 million tonnes in 2024. It also accommodates 1.7 million ferry passengers annually via routes to [Cairnryan](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cairnryan) and [Liverpool](https://grokipedia.com/page/Liverpool), underscoring its role in sustaining cross-border supply chains and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism). The port's strategic location drives economic resilience, with cargo volumes rising 0.6% year-on-year amid global trade fluctuations.[[[27]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-27)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-27)[[[28]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-28)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-28)**Carlingford Lough**, a shared border estuary between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, hosts smaller-scale operations focused on fishing and modest cargo handling, with joint management ensuring cross-jurisdictional cooperation. Facilities here emphasize sustainable fisheries and limited bulk imports, supporting local coastal communities without significant industrial-scale throughput.**Drogheda Port** in [County Louth](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Louth) operates as a Tier 2 facility dedicated to [bulk cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bulk_cargo) such as [cement](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cement), fertilizers, grains, and agri-products, with principal commodities including timber and [steel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Steel). Its annual capacity supports around 1.5 million tonnes, positioning it as a vital link for northeast Ireland's agricultural and [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing) exports via deepwater berths on the River Boyne. The port prioritizes [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics) efficiency for project and outsized [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), enhancing regional supply chains.[[[29]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-29)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-29)**[Dublin Port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin_Port)**, Ireland's busiest harbor and a Tier 1 asset in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin), manages 35.2 million tonnes of cargo annually in 2024, encompassing unitised goods, oil, and bulk imports critical to national [EU](https://grokipedia.com/page/.eu) trade. It also facilitates 1.6 million ferry passengers, primarily on routes to [Holyhead](https://grokipedia.com/page/Holyhead), [Wales](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wales), reinforcing its centrality in passenger mobility and freight corridors. As the primary entry point for over half of Ireland's seaborne trade, the port drives economic integration while investing in sustainable infrastructure.[[[8]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)[[[30]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-30)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-30)**Dún Laoghaire Harbour** in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin) primarily serves as a passenger and yachting facility, hosting ferry services to [Holyhead](https://grokipedia.com/page/Holyhead) (though reduced in recent years) and welcoming over 137,000 cruise passengers across 80 ship calls in 2024. Lacking commercial cargo operations, it focuses on leisure maritime activities, including sailing events and [marina](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marina) services, while acting as a key tourism hub adjacent to [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) city.[[[31]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-31)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-31)[[[32]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-32)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-32)**Greenore Port**, a deepwater terminal in [County Louth](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Louth) on Carlingford Lough, specializes in containers and bulk [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) like fertilizers and animal feeds, with a capacity supporting up to 2 million tonnes annually. Managed as part of the broader lough infrastructure, it enables efficient Ro-Ro and [lift-on/lift-off](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lift-on/lift-off) operations, contributing to Ireland's import needs for agriculture and industry near the Dublin-Belfast corridor.**Howth Harbour** in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin) functions mainly as a [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and leisure port, accommodating a fleet of around 100 vessels and serving as a base for Ireland's east coast whitefish and [shellfish](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shellfish) landings. It supports recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism), with no major commercial [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) role, emphasizing [sustainable fishery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sustainable_fishery) practices and coastal heritage.**Malahide Marina**, located in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin), is a recreational [yacht](https://grokipedia.com/page/Yacht) harbor with over 300 berths, dedicated exclusively to [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure)[sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) and [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) without any commercial or [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations. It caters to private vessels and watersports, integrated into the local [marina](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marina) network for non-industrial maritime [recreation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Recreation).
### North Coast Ports

The north coast of Ireland, stretching from [Lough Foyle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Foyle) to [Belfast Lough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast_Lough), features a series of smaller harbors and marinas that primarily support [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations, recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating), and limited regional freight, with a notable concentration in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland). These ports play a vital role in local economies, facilitating whitefish landings, [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure) tourism, and cross-channel trade, particularly with [Scotland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scotland) via the North Channel. Unlike larger facilities elsewhere, they emphasize community-based activities and niche cargo like aggregates and bulk commodities, contributing to coastal resilience amid seasonal demands.[[[33]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)Ballycastle Harbour, located in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, serves as a small fishing and tourism port with a focus on leisure craft. It includes a 74-berth Blue Flag marina in its inner basin, offering sheltered pontoon berthing for visiting vessels and supporting local angling and small-scale fishing activities. The harbor's position on the northeast coast enhances its appeal for recreational sailors exploring the Causeway Coast.[[[34]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-34)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-34)[[[35]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-35)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-35)Bangor Marina, in [County Down](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Down), [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), functions exclusively as a yacht and recreational facility without cargo operations, bolstering coastal [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) through high-end marine services. As [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland)'s largest and most prestigious marina, it provides 24-hour access to facilities including toilets, showers, self-service fuelling, and a clubhouse, attracting over 1,500 visiting boats annually. Its sheltered location in [Belfast Lough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast_Lough) makes it a hub for leisure sailing and supports regional [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) by accommodating superyachts and day trippers.[[[36]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-36)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-36)[[[37]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-37)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-37)[[[38]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-38)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-38)Coleraine Port, situated on the River Bann in County Londonderry, Northern Ireland, operates as a minor commercial harbor specializing in aggregates and other bulk cargoes with low annual tonnage. It features three 217-meter quays, two transit sheds totaling 1,912 square meters, and a single 18-tonne capacity crane for handling general cargo, agricultural products, and construction materials via approximately 50 coaster calls per year. Handling around 75,000 tonnes as of recent records, the port supports local trade without deep-sea capabilities.[[[39]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-39)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-39)[[[40]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-40)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-40)[[[41]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-41)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-41)Greencastle Harbour in [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal) stands as a key [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) port, recognized as Ireland's largest whitefish landing center with annual catches approaching 10,000 tonnes, primarily from demersal species. Managed under the oversight of Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), it sustains a robust local [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) economy, employing hundreds in processing and related sectors while contributing nearly 22% of port-area jobs in [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing). The harbor's protected position at Lough Foyle's entrance facilitates efficient landings for trawlers, underscoring its role in national [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) resilience despite fluctuations in foreign vessel activity.[[[42]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-42)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-42)[[[43]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-43)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-43)[[[44]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)Londonderry Port, also known as Foyle Port on the River Foyle in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), functions as the region's primary commercial facility, handling a record 2.5 million tonnes of freight in 2024/25 with a focus on bulk commodities and regional trade to [Scotland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scotland). It offers turn-key services including stevedoring, craneage, storage, and marine operations like dredging and towage, processing a mix of dry and liquid bulks through dedicated terminals. Recent growth has seen turnover rise 25% to £15.22 million, reflecting expanded freight volumes and its strategic position for North West trade.[[[33]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)[[[45]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-45)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-45)[[[46]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-46)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-46)Portrush Harbour in [County Antrim](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Antrim), [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), combines tourism and small-scale fishing functions, accommodating commercial vessels, yachts, and angling boats within its breakwater-protected basin. It supports leisure activities such as sea fishing trips and wildlife tours, drawing visitors to the Causeway Coast while hosting a fleet of colorful trawlers and creel boats for local catches. The harbor's vibrant promenade enhances its role in seasonal tourism, providing docking for operators offering mackerel angling and coastal excursions.[[[47]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-47)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-47)[[[48]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-48)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-48)[[[49]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-49)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-49)Rathmullan Pier in [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal) operates as a small passenger and [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) point, connecting to nearby areas across [Lough Swilly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Swilly) for local transport. It serves as the Rathmullan terminal for the seasonal [Lough Swilly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Swilly)[Ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry), which runs daily from late May to [September](https://grokipedia.com/page/September), carrying up to 18 [vehicles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aston_Martin_VH_platform) and over 100 passengers per [sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) on a 40-minute route to [Buncrana](https://grokipedia.com/page/Buncrana). This service, operated by Cara na nOileán Teo, facilitates [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) and commuter links in the Fanad Peninsula region without cargo handling.[[[50]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-50)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-50)[[[51]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-51)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-51)[[[52]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-52)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-52)
### West Coast Ports

The west coast ports of Ireland, stretching from Donegal in the northwest to Kerry in the southwest, play a vital role in supporting regional economies through [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing), local [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) handling, and [passenger](https://grokipedia.com/page/Passenger) services to offshore islands. Exposed to the Atlantic Ocean, these harbors often prioritize resilient infrastructure for harsh weather conditions and focus on niche activities like seafood processing and emerging offshore renewable energy support, rather than large-scale [international trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/International_trade). Many are designated as fishery harbor centers by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, facilitating sustainable [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations and community livelihoods.**Killybegs Harbour**, located in Bertraghboy Bay, [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal), stands as Ireland's premier fishing port and one of Europe's largest for remote-water fleets. It processes a significant portion of the nation's [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) landings, with 166,423 tonnes reported in 2023, though 2024 figures show a drop to 82,000 tonnes of fish for human consumption due to market and quota pressures. The port supports around 1,500 direct and indirect jobs in processing and logistics, underscoring its economic backbone for the northwest region.[[[44]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)[[[53]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-53)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-53)**Galway Port**, a Tier 2 commercial facility in [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway), serves as the primary hub for the west coast, handling diverse cargo including aggregates, timber, and project cargoes for construction. In 2022, it managed 500,259 tonnes of goods, with 287,990 tonnes imported and 212,269 tonnes exported, while also operating ferry services to the [Aran Islands](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aran_Islands) that carry thousands of passengers annually. The port is positioning itself for offshore wind development, having handled components for 20% of Ireland's onshore wind turbines between 2013 and 2023 and exploring floating wind opportunities in Galway Bay.[[[54]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-54)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-54)[[[55]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-55)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-55)[[[56]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-56)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-56)**Westport Harbour** in [County Mayo](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Mayo) specializes in regional exports like timber and livestock, contributing to the area's agricultural trade. It accommodates vessels up to certain deadweights for [short-sea shipping](https://grokipedia.com/page/Short-sea_shipping) and supports local fishing fleets, though specific annual tonnages remain modest compared to national averages, aligning with its role in serving Mayo's rural economy. The harbor also features leisure facilities, enhancing tourism along [Clew Bay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clew_Bay).[[[57]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-57)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-57)**Fenit Harbour**, near [Tralee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tralee) in [County Kerry](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Kerry), functions as a multipurpose regional port handling agri-exports, general cargo, and fishing. In 2022, it processed approximately 24,000 tonnes, primarily [Liebherr](https://grokipedia.com/page/Liebherr) crane components from nearby manufacturing, alongside 18 vessel calls annually. Its deep-water access supports vessels up to 17,000 DWT, making it a key link for Kerry's export-oriented industries.[[[58]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-58)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-58)[[[59]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-59)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-59)Smaller harbors like **[Belmullet (Blacksod Bay)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belmullet)** in [County Mayo](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Mayo) provide essential support for offshore surveys, [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing), and meteorological operations, with its pier serving as a base for Atlantic research vessels and local pelagic fleets. The remote location aids in monitoring weather patterns critical for transatlantic shipping.**Burrishoole Harbour** near Newport, also in Mayo, operates primarily as a small [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and leisure facility, accommodating local boats for [angling](https://grokipedia.com/page/Angling) and recreational [sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) along Clew Bay's [estuary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Estuary). Its historical significance as a medieval [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) point persists in its community-focused role today.[[[60]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-60)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-60)**Clifden Boat Harbour** in [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway) emphasizes tourism, offering berths for leisure craft and serving as a gateway for [Connemara](https://grokipedia.com/page/Connemara) coastal exploration, without notable cargo operations. It supports seasonal visitor boats and aligns with the region's [ecotourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ecotourism) initiatives.Island-access ports include **Inishbofin Harbour** off [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway), which handles [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) services from the mainland and small-scale fishing, connecting the island's 200 residents to essential supplies. Similarly, **Tarbert Island** in [County Kerry](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Kerry) acts as a minor cargo and [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) terminal, facilitating cross-Shannon services and local maritime traffic.

### South Coast Ports

The south coast ports of Ireland, stretching along the [Celtic Sea](https://grokipedia.com/page/Celtic_Sea) from [County Waterford](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Waterford) to [County Cork](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Cork), serve as essential gateways for [bulk cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bulk_cargo) handling, energy imports via specialized oil terminals, and a burgeoning cruise tourism sector that attracts international visitors to historic sites and coastal attractions. These facilities support diverse economic activities, including fisheries, Ro-Ro freight, and agricultural exports, contributing to regional trade while leveraging natural deepwater advantages for larger vessels. Key ports in this region emphasize [energy security](https://grokipedia.com/page/Energy_security), seafood processing, and passenger connectivity to continental Europe and the UK.**Bantry Harbour**, operated by Bantry Bay Port Company, functions as a deepwater [oil terminal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Oil_terminal) on the southwest coast, primarily facilitating oil transhipment and storage at the adjacent [Whiddy Island](https://grokipedia.com/page/Whiddy_Island) facility, which supports Ireland's energy imports through secure handling of [petroleum](https://grokipedia.com/page/Petroleum) products. The port's infrastructure accommodates large tankers in a sheltered [bay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bay) with depths up to [30](https://grokipedia.com/page/-30-) meters, enabling efficient operations for bulk liquid cargo essential to national fuel supplies.[[[61]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-61)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-61)[[[62]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-62)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-62)**Castletownbere Harbour** in [County Cork](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Cork) stands as Ireland's second-largest [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood)[port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Port) and a major hub for whitefish landings, processing over 27,000 tonnes of fish valued at €96 million in 2023, underscoring its role as Europe's largest remote [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing)[port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Port). The facility supports a robust [commercial fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Commercial_fishing) fleet and associated industries like [aquaculture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aquaculture) and processing, generating significant local [employment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Employment) and economic impact through high-volume [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) exports.[[[63]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-63)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-63)[[[64]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-64)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-64)**Cobh**, part of the Port of Cork complex, operates as a premier cruise and passenger terminal with Ireland's only dedicated cruise berth, welcoming approximately 100 cruise ship calls annually and over 180,000 passengers in recent seasons, boosting tourism through proximity to landmarks like the Cobh Heritage Centre. The 350-meter berth at depths of 9.1 meters allows direct access for large vessels, integrating seamlessly with shore excursions focused on maritime history and regional heritage.[[[65]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-65)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-65)[[[66]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-66)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-66)**Dunmore East Harbour** in [County Waterford](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Waterford) serves as a key [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing)[port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Port), accommodating a local fleet that includes pelagic vessels and supporting commercial seafood operations with modern facilities for landings and processing. As one of Ireland's designated fishery harbour centres, it handles diverse catches while providing safe berthing for offshore trawlers, contributing to the southeast's maritime economy.[[[14]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)[[[67]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-67)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-67)**Kinsale Harbour** in [County Cork](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Cork) functions as a small-scale [yacht](https://grokipedia.com/page/Yacht) and [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) harbor, featuring a [marina](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marina) with berths for leisure craft alongside a working fleet for deep-sea [angling](https://grokipedia.com/page/Angling) and local charters targeting species like [cod](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cod) and [sharks](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sharks!). authority ports, and other harbours, with major facilities like [Dublin Port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin_Port) and Port of Cork dominating freight annually via ferries and cruises.[[[2]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-2)[[[3]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-3)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-3)[[[4]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-4)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-4) In 2024, throughput increased to 51 million tonnes, a 7% rise, driven by growth in dry bulk and Ro-Ro sectors amid expanding roles in offshore ## Background

### Port Classification

A port in Ireland is defined as a maritime facility equipped to handle [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), passengers, [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) vessels, or recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) activities, serving as a critical interface between sea and land transport networks.Under Ireland's National Ports Policy, established in 2013 and subject to an ongoing review process initiated in 2023, with the final revised policy anticipated in the first half of [2026](https://grokipedia.com/page/2026), commercial ports are classified into tiers based on their scale, trade volume, and national importance. Tier 1 ports, designated for national and international significance, include Dublin Port Company, Port of Cork Company, and Shannon Foynes Port Company; these facilities collectively handle the majority of the country's freight and passenger traffic. Tier 2 ports, focused on regional significance and supporting competitive markets in specific sectors, comprise Port of Waterford Company and [Rosslare Europort](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rosslare_Europort). Additional commercial ports of regional importance, such as [Drogheda](https://grokipedia.com/page/Drogheda) Port Company and Galway Harbour Company, fall outside the Tier 1 and Tier 2 categories but contribute to localized trade and logistics.[[[11]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)[[[12]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-12)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-12)[[[13]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-13)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-13)Beyond the tiered commercial ports, Ireland recognizes specialized classifications for other maritime facilities. Fishing harbors, known as Fishery Harbour Centres, are designated and managed by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine to support sea fishing, fish processing, and related activities; examples include Killybegs and Castletownbere, which are maintained as multi-purpose assets for the fishing industry. Yacht marinas and recreational harbors cater primarily to leisure boating and are often operated by local authorities or private entities, emphasizing berthing and support services rather than commercial cargo. Cruise terminals, integrated within larger commercial ports, are equipped for passenger vessels and tourism, with facilities designed for efficient embarkation and shore excursions.[[[14]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-14)[[[15]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-15)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-15)In [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), ports are overseen by the Department for Infrastructure without a formal tier system akin to the Republic's policy, instead categorized broadly as commercial or local harbors to facilitate [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) and regional connectivity. Major commercial ports, such as [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) Harbour and [Larne](https://grokipedia.com/page/Larne) Harbour, function as key [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) gateways handling significant cargo and passenger volumes, while smaller local harbors support fishing and community needs; trust ports like [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) and [Warrenpoint](https://grokipedia.com/page/Warrenpoint) operate under statutory oversight to ensure public benefit.[[[16]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-16)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-16)[[[17]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-17)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-17)The classification criteria for Irish ports emphasize quantitative and qualitative factors, including annual [tonnage](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tonnage) handled—typically with Tier 1 ports exceeding several million tonnes—to gauge economic impact, alongside [infrastructure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infrastructure) attributes like [water](https://grokipedia.com/page/Water) depth for vessel access (often 10-15 meters or more for larger ports) and strategic positioning within [EU](https://grokipedia.com/page/.eu) trade corridors. These elements ensure ports align with national objectives for efficient [maritime transport](https://grokipedia.com/page/Maritime_transport) and resilience in global supply chains.[[[11]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-11)[[[18]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-18)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-18)
### Economic and Strategic Importance

Irish ports serve as the primary conduits for the country's external trade, handling over 95% of merchandise by volume as an island nation reliant on maritime logistics. In 2024, total [goods](https://grokipedia.com/page/Goods) throughput across major ports reached 51 million tonnes, reflecting a 7% increase from the previous year and underscoring the sector's resilience amid global [supply chain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Supply_chain) pressures.[[[19]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-19)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-19) This volume includes a mix of bulk commodities, containerized [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), and roll-on/roll-off traffic essential for Ireland's export-driven economy.The maritime sector, which includes port operations, shipping, and ancillary services, makes a substantial contribution to [Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ireland)'s GDP. Valued at €2.7 billion in [gross value added](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gross_value_added) in 2023 (up from €1.6 billion in 2021), it supports approximately 20,000 direct jobs and underpins annual trade flows exceeding €100 billion, primarily through imports of raw materials and exports of high-value goods like pharmaceuticals and agri-products. These activities not only drive [regional development](https://grokipedia.com/page/Regional_development) but also enhance national competitiveness by connecting [Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ireland) to global markets.[[[20]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-20)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-20)Strategically, Irish ports have evolved as critical gateways for EU-UK trade following [Brexit](https://grokipedia.com/page/Brexit), managing rerouted flows and maintaining seamless supply chains under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. They also facilitate vital ferry links to Britain and continental Europe, carrying around 4 million passengers annually and supporting tourism and short-sea shipping. Emerging as hubs for offshore wind energy, ports are positioning to support Ireland's target of 5 GW installed capacity by 2030, with infrastructure upgrades enabling assembly, maintenance, and deployment of renewable projects.[[[21]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-21)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-21)[[[22]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-22)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-22)In [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), ports handle approximately 95% of the region's external trade, with [Belfast](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast) Harbour alone processing 24.1 million tonnes in 2024, a slight rise from the prior year and vital for cross-border and international commerce. This throughput bolsters local industries and mitigates economic isolation post-Brexit.[[[9]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-9)[[[23]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-23)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-23)Looking ahead, Irish ports face challenges like decarbonization, with initiatives such as [shore power](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shore_power) adoption at facilities like [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) and Rosslare aimed at reducing emissions from idling vessels through EU-funded projects. Efforts to mitigate port congestion include capacity expansions and digitalization, while alignment with the EU's [Trans-European Transport Network](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trans-European_Transport_Network) (TEN-T) grants core and comprehensive status to key ports, unlocking funding for sustainable upgrades.[[[24]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-24)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-24)[[[25]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-25)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-25)
## Ports by Coastal Region

### East Coast Ports

The east coast ports of Ireland, bordering the [Irish Sea](https://grokipedia.com/page/Irish_Sea), serve as vital gateways for passenger ferries linking the island to Britain and for industrial cargo transport, including bulk commodities, containers, and roll-on/roll-off (Ro-Ro) freight essential to EU-UK [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) routes. These facilities, ranging from major commercial hubs to specialized [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure) harbors, handle a significant portion of Ireland's maritime activity, with emphasis on efficient cross-sea connectivity and support for sectors like [construction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Construction), [agriculture](https://grokipedia.com/page/Agriculture), and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism). Ports in this region benefit from proximity to Dublin's [economic corridor](https://grokipedia.com/page/Economic_corridor), facilitating just-in-time [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics) while facing challenges from tidal constraints and urban development pressures.**Arklow Port**, situated in [County Wicklow](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Wicklow) midway between [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) and Rosslare, functions as a commercial harbor primarily serving the maritime industry with dry bulk trade, including timber and aggregates for [construction](https://grokipedia.com/page/Construction). It supports local shipping operations and offshore activities, such as servicing the nearby Arklow Bank windfarm, though its depth limitations restrict larger vessels. The port is managed by Wicklow [County Council](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_council) and remains a key asset for regional export-import flows.[[[26]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-26)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-26)**Belfast Port** in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland) stands as one of the region's premier commercial facilities, specializing in Ro-Ro freight to Britain, containers, and [bulk cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bulk_cargo) like [coal](https://grokipedia.com/page/Coal) and [grain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Grain), with an annual throughput of 24.1 million tonnes in 2024. It also accommodates 1.7 million ferry passengers annually via routes to [Cairnryan](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cairnryan) and [Liverpool](https://grokipedia.com/page/Liverpool), underscoring its role in sustaining cross-border supply chains and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism). The port's strategic location drives economic resilience, with cargo volumes rising 0.6% year-on-year amid global trade fluctuations.[[[27]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-27)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-27)[[[28]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-28)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-28)**Carlingford Lough**, a shared border estuary between the Republic of Ireland and Northern Ireland, hosts smaller-scale operations focused on fishing and modest cargo handling, with joint management ensuring cross-jurisdictional cooperation. Facilities here emphasize sustainable fisheries and limited bulk imports, supporting local coastal communities without significant industrial-scale throughput.**Drogheda Port** in [County Louth](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Louth) operates as a Tier 2 facility dedicated to [bulk cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bulk_cargo) such as [cement](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cement), fertilizers, grains, and agri-products, with principal commodities including timber and [steel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Steel). Its annual capacity supports around 1.5 million tonnes, positioning it as a vital link for northeast Ireland's agricultural and [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing) exports via deepwater berths on the River Boyne. The port prioritizes [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics) efficiency for project and outsized [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo), enhancing regional supply chains.[[[29]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-29)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-29)**[Dublin Port](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin_Port)**, Ireland's busiest harbor and a Tier 1 asset in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin), manages 35.2 million tonnes of cargo annually in 2024, encompassing unitised goods, oil, and bulk imports critical to national [EU](https://grokipedia.com/page/.eu) trade. It also facilitates 1.6 million ferry passengers, primarily on routes to [Holyhead](https://grokipedia.com/page/Holyhead), [Wales](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wales), reinforcing its centrality in passenger mobility and freight corridors. As the primary entry point for over half of Ireland's seaborne trade, the port drives economic integration while investing in sustainable infrastructure.[[[8]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-8)[[[30]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-30)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-30)**Dún Laoghaire Harbour** in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin) primarily serves as a passenger and yachting facility, hosting ferry services to [Holyhead](https://grokipedia.com/page/Holyhead) (though reduced in recent years) and welcoming over 137,000 cruise passengers across 80 ship calls in 2024. Lacking commercial cargo operations, it focuses on leisure maritime activities, including sailing events and [marina](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marina) services, while acting as a key tourism hub adjacent to [Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dublin) city.[[[31]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-31)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-31)[[[32]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-32)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-32)**Greenore Port**, a deepwater terminal in [County Louth](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Louth) on Carlingford Lough, specializes in containers and bulk [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) like fertilizers and animal feeds, with a capacity supporting up to 2 million tonnes annually. Managed as part of the broader lough infrastructure, it enables efficient Ro-Ro and [lift-on/lift-off](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lift-on/lift-off) operations, contributing to Ireland's import needs for agriculture and industry near the Dublin-Belfast corridor.**Howth Harbour** in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin) functions mainly as a [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and leisure port, accommodating a fleet of around 100 vessels and serving as a base for Ireland's east coast whitefish and [shellfish](https://grokipedia.com/page/Shellfish) landings. It supports recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) and [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism), with no major commercial [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) role, emphasizing [sustainable fishery](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sustainable_fishery) practices and coastal heritage.**Malahide Marina**, located in [County Dublin](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Dublin), is a recreational [yacht](https://grokipedia.com/page/Yacht) harbor with over 300 berths, dedicated exclusively to [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure)[sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) and [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating) without any commercial or [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations. It caters to private vessels and watersports, integrated into the local [marina](https://grokipedia.com/page/Marina) network for non-industrial maritime [recreation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Recreation).
### North Coast Ports

The north coast of Ireland, stretching from [Lough Foyle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Foyle) to [Belfast Lough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast_Lough), features a series of smaller harbors and marinas that primarily support [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations, recreational [boating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Boating), and limited regional freight, with a notable concentration in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland). These ports play a vital role in local economies, facilitating whitefish landings, [leisure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Leisure) tourism, and cross-channel trade, particularly with [Scotland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scotland) via the North Channel. Unlike larger facilities elsewhere, they emphasize community-based activities and niche cargo like aggregates and bulk commodities, contributing to coastal resilience amid seasonal demands.[[[33]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)Ballycastle Harbour, located in County Antrim, Northern Ireland, serves as a small fishing and tourism port with a focus on leisure craft. It includes a 74-berth Blue Flag marina in its inner basin, offering sheltered pontoon berthing for visiting vessels and supporting local angling and small-scale fishing activities. The harbor's position on the northeast coast enhances its appeal for recreational sailors exploring the Causeway Coast.[[[34]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-34)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-34)[[[35]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-35)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-35)Bangor Marina, in [County Down](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Down), [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), functions exclusively as a yacht and recreational facility without cargo operations, bolstering coastal [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) through high-end marine services. As [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland)'s largest and most prestigious marina, it provides 24-hour access to facilities including toilets, showers, self-service fuelling, and a clubhouse, attracting over 1,500 visiting boats annually. Its sheltered location in [Belfast Lough](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belfast_Lough) makes it a hub for leisure sailing and supports regional [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) by accommodating superyachts and day trippers.[[[36]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-36)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-36)[[[37]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-37)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-37)[[[38]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-38)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-38)Coleraine Port, situated on the River Bann in County Londonderry, Northern Ireland, operates as a minor commercial harbor specializing in aggregates and other bulk cargoes with low annual tonnage. It features three 217-meter quays, two transit sheds totaling 1,912 square meters, and a single 18-tonne capacity crane for handling general cargo, agricultural products, and construction materials via approximately 50 coaster calls per year. Handling around 75,000 tonnes as of recent records, the port supports local trade without deep-sea capabilities.[[[39]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-39)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-39)[[[40]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-40)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-40)[[[41]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-41)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-41)Greencastle Harbour in [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal) stands as a key [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) port, recognized as Ireland's largest whitefish landing center with annual catches approaching 10,000 tonnes, primarily from demersal species. Managed under the oversight of Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM), it sustains a robust local [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) economy, employing hundreds in processing and related sectors while contributing nearly 22% of port-area jobs in [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing). The harbor's protected position at Lough Foyle's entrance facilitates efficient landings for trawlers, underscoring its role in national [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) resilience despite fluctuations in foreign vessel activity.[[[42]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-42)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-42)[[[43]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-43)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-43)[[[44]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)Londonderry Port, also known as Foyle Port on the River Foyle in [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), functions as the region's primary commercial facility, handling a record 2.5 million tonnes of freight in 2024/25 with a focus on bulk commodities and regional trade to [Scotland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Scotland). It offers turn-key services including stevedoring, craneage, storage, and marine operations like dredging and towage, processing a mix of dry and liquid bulks through dedicated terminals. Recent growth has seen turnover rise 25% to £15.22 million, reflecting expanded freight volumes and its strategic position for North West trade.[[[33]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-33)[[[45]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-45)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-45)[[[46]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-46)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-46)Portrush Harbour in [County Antrim](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Antrim), [Northern Ireland](https://grokipedia.com/page/Northern_Ireland), combines tourism and small-scale fishing functions, accommodating commercial vessels, yachts, and angling boats within its breakwater-protected basin. It supports leisure activities such as sea fishing trips and wildlife tours, drawing visitors to the Causeway Coast while hosting a fleet of colorful trawlers and creel boats for local catches. The harbor's vibrant promenade enhances its role in seasonal tourism, providing docking for operators offering mackerel angling and coastal excursions.[[[47]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-47)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-47)[[[48]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-48)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-48)[[[49]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-49)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-49)Rathmullan Pier in [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal) operates as a small passenger and [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) point, connecting to nearby areas across [Lough Swilly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Swilly) for local transport. It serves as the Rathmullan terminal for the seasonal [Lough Swilly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Lough_Swilly)[Ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry), which runs daily from late May to [September](https://grokipedia.com/page/September), carrying up to 18 [vehicles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aston_Martin_VH_platform) and over 100 passengers per [sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) on a 40-minute route to [Buncrana](https://grokipedia.com/page/Buncrana). This service, operated by Cara na nOileán Teo, facilitates [tourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tourism) and commuter links in the Fanad Peninsula region without cargo handling.[[[50]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-50)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-50)[[[51]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-51)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-51)[[[52]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-52)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-52)
### West Coast Ports

The west coast ports of Ireland, stretching from Donegal in the northwest to Kerry in the southwest, play a vital role in supporting regional economies through [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing), local [cargo](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cargo) handling, and [passenger](https://grokipedia.com/page/Passenger) services to offshore islands. Exposed to the Atlantic Ocean, these harbors often prioritize resilient infrastructure for harsh weather conditions and focus on niche activities like seafood processing and emerging offshore renewable energy support, rather than large-scale [international trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/International_trade). Many are designated as fishery harbor centers by the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine, facilitating sustainable [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) operations and community livelihoods.**Killybegs Harbour**, located in Bertraghboy Bay, [County Donegal](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Donegal), stands as Ireland's premier fishing port and one of Europe's largest for remote-water fleets. It processes a significant portion of the nation's [seafood](https://grokipedia.com/page/Seafood) landings, with 166,423 tonnes reported in 2023, though 2024 figures show a drop to 82,000 tonnes of fish for human consumption due to market and quota pressures. The port supports around 1,500 direct and indirect jobs in processing and logistics, underscoring its economic backbone for the northwest region.[[[44]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-44)[[[53]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-53)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-53)**Galway Port**, a Tier 2 commercial facility in [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway), serves as the primary hub for the west coast, handling diverse cargo including aggregates, timber, and project cargoes for construction. In 2022, it managed 500,259 tonnes of goods, with 287,990 tonnes imported and 212,269 tonnes exported, while also operating ferry services to the [Aran Islands](https://grokipedia.com/page/Aran_Islands) that carry thousands of passengers annually. The port is positioning itself for offshore wind development, having handled components for 20% of Ireland's onshore wind turbines between 2013 and 2023 and exploring floating wind opportunities in Galway Bay.[[[54]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-54)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-54)[[[55]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-55)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-55)[[[56]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-56)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-56)**Westport Harbour** in [County Mayo](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Mayo) specializes in regional exports like timber and livestock, contributing to the area's agricultural trade. It accommodates vessels up to certain deadweights for [short-sea shipping](https://grokipedia.com/page/Short-sea_shipping) and supports local fishing fleets, though specific annual tonnages remain modest compared to national averages, aligning with its role in serving Mayo's rural economy. The harbor also features leisure facilities, enhancing tourism along [Clew Bay](https://grokipedia.com/page/Clew_Bay).[[[57]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-57)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-57)**Fenit Harbour**, near [Tralee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tralee) in [County Kerry](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Kerry), functions as a multipurpose regional port handling agri-exports, general cargo, and fishing. In 2022, it processed approximately 24,000 tonnes, primarily [Liebherr](https://grokipedia.com/page/Liebherr) crane components from nearby manufacturing, alongside 18 vessel calls annually. Its deep-water access supports vessels up to 17,000 DWT, making it a key link for Kerry's export-oriented industries.[[[58]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-58)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-58)[[[59]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-59)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-59)Smaller harbors like **[Belmullet (Blacksod Bay)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Belmullet)** in [County Mayo](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Mayo) provide essential support for offshore surveys, [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing), and meteorological operations, with its pier serving as a base for Atlantic research vessels and local pelagic fleets. The remote location aids in monitoring weather patterns critical for transatlantic shipping.**Burrishoole Harbour** near Newport, also in Mayo, operates primarily as a small [fishing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fishing) and leisure facility, accommodating local boats for [angling](https://grokipedia.com/page/Angling) and recreational [sailing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sailing) along Clew Bay's [estuary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Estuary). Its historical significance as a medieval [trade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Trade) point persists in its community-focused role today.[[[60]](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-60)](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_ports_in_Ireland#ref-60)**Clifden Boat Harbour** in [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway) emphasizes tourism, offering berths for leisure craft and serving as a gateway for [Connemara](https://grokipedia.com/page/Connemara) coastal exploration, without notable cargo operations. It supports seasonal visitor boats and aligns with the region's [ecotourism](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ecotourism) initiatives.Island-access ports include **Inishbofin Harbour** off [County Galway](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Galway), which handles [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) services from the mainland and small-scale fishing, connecting the island's 200 residents to essential supplies. Similarly, **Tarbert Island** in [County Kerry](https://grokipedia.com/page/County_Kerry) acts as a minor cargo and [ferry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ferry) terminal, facilitating cross-Shannon services and local maritime traffic.
